claim: Wegener was ridiculed. The president of the American Philosophical Society called drift 'utter, damned rot', another American said accepting it meant forgetting 70 years of learning, and Wegener could not get a professorship at any German university.
spoken_form: The reaction was brutal. One society president called it utter, damned rot. Another scientist said believing it meant forgetting everything geologists had learned in seventy years.
source_title: NASA Earth Observatory / NASA Science, 'Alfred Wegener'
quote: "Utter, damned rot!" said the president of the prestigious American Philosophical Society. "If we are to believe [this] hypothesis, we must forget everything we have learned in the last 70 years and start all over again," said another American scientist. ... Because of this abuse, Wegener could not get a professorship at any German university.
caveat: These quotes are widely repeated, but I did not check the primary sources. The '70 years' line is usually credited to R. T. Chamberlin at the AAPG New York symposium (15 Nov 1926; proceedings published 1928). Don't name the speakers on screen without a primary source. Graz (Austria) made Wegener a professor in 1924.

claim: The main objection was the missing force. Wegener's candidates, a centrifugal 'flight from the poles' and tidal forces, were too weak. In his 1929 edition he admitted, 'The Newton of drift theory has not yet appeared.' Mantle convection, which he also discussed, is today's leading candidate.
spoken_form: Critics had one killer question: what could possibly push a continent? Wegener guessed Earth's spin and tides. Both were far too weak. He admitted it himself: the Newton of drift theory has not yet appeared.
display: 'THE NEWTON OF DRIFT ... NOT YET APPEARED'
source_title: NASA Earth Observatory / NASA Science, 'Alfred Wegener'
quote: His major problem was finding a force or forces that could make the continents "plow around in the mantle," as one critic put it. Wegener tentatively suggested two candidates: centrifugal force caused by the rotation of the Earth, and tidal-type waves in the Earth itself ... "The Newton of drift theory has not yet appeared."
caveat: The rotation-based force is Wegener's 'Polflucht' (flight from the poles), the idea Holden parodied. Harold Jeffreys showed these forces were far too small.

claim: Wegener died on the Greenland ice sheet in November 1930. The last photo shows him leaving the mid-ice station Eismitte on 1 November 1930, his 50th birthday. His body was found on 12 May 1931; his companion Rasmus Villumsen was never found.
spoken_form: On his fiftieth birthday, Wegener left a camp in the middle of the Greenland ice. He never made it back. They found his body the next May, carefully buried in the snow by his companion, who vanished into the ice.
source_title: NASA Earth Observatory / NASA Science, 'Alfred Wegener'
quote: The last photo of Alfred Wegener and Rasmus Villumsen, taken on 1 November 1930 (Wegener's 50th birthday) as they were leaving the "Eismitte" Station. ... On May 12, 1931, they found Wegener's body. ... Though a long, exhaustive search was made, the faithful Greenlander's body was never found.
caveat: The exact date of death is unknown (mid to late November 1930); the presumed cause is heart failure from overexertion. The photos on the NASA page are (c) AWI, not public domain.

claim: The proof came from the seafloor. From the 1950s on, magnetometers found 'zebra' stripes of normal and reversed magnetism running parallel to the mid-ocean ridges, mirrored on both sides. Vine and Matthews (Nature, September 1963) explained them as seafloor spreading, 33 years after Wegener's death.
spoken_form: The proof was hiding on the ocean floor: stripes of magnetized rock, mirrored on both sides of the mid-ocean ridges, like a tape recording of new seafloor being made. It was published in nineteen sixty-three, thirty-three years after Wegener died.
source_title: USGS, This Dynamic Earth, 'Developing the theory'; Vine, F. J. & Matthews, D. H. (1963), Magnetic Anomalies Over Oceanic Ridges, Nature 199: 947-949
quote: By explaining both the zebralike magnetic striping and the construction of the mid-ocean ridge system, the seafloor spreading hypothesis quickly gained converts and represented another major advance in the development of the plate-tectonics theory.
caveat: Vine-Matthews citation verified via Crossref (Nature 199(4897): 947-949, Sept 1963). Lawrence Morley reached the same idea independently, and Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading in 1962. '33 years' = 1963 minus 1930.

claim: In reconstructions of Gondwana, Antarctica is the centrepiece, with South America, Africa, India and Australia fitted around it. Geologists have called it the 'keypiece' of Gondwana since Du Toit's 1937 book.
spoken_form: Run the clock back and the southern continents lock together into one supercontinent, Gondwana. At its heart sits Antarctica. Geologists call it the keypiece.
source_title: Dalziel, I. W. D. (2013). Antarctica and supercontinental evolution: clues and puzzles. Earth and Environmental Science Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 104: 3-16 (abstract via Crossref)
quote: Antarctica has been known as the "keypiece" of the Gondwana supercontinent since publication of Du Toit's 1937 classic book Our Wandering Continents.
caveat: NASA's Wegener feature adds that once Africa, Antarctica, Australia and India are put back together as Gondwanaland, the Permo-Carboniferous glacial deposits 'clustered neatly around the South Pole'.

claim: Gondwana began tearing apart in the Jurassic. Huge Karoo-Ferrar lava floods around 183 million years ago came first. The first ocean crust between Africa and Antarctica formed about 155 million years ago, and South America and Africa had fully split from Antarctica by the Early Cretaceous (chron M14N).
spoken_form: It started in the age of dinosaurs. About a hundred and fifty-five million years ago, the first sliver of new ocean opened between Africa and Antarctica.
source_title: Jokat, W., Boebel, T., Konig, M. & Meyer, U. (2003). Timing and geometry of early Gondwana breakup. Journal of Geophysical Research 108(B9), doi:10.1029/2002JB001802
quote: In the Riiser-Larsen Sea/Mozambique Basin, the first oceanic crust between Africa and Antarctica formed around 155 Ma. ... At chron M14N, South America and Africa finally were split off the Antarctic continent.
caveat: Ages depend on which magnetic timescale is used. Duncan et al. (1997, JGR 102: 18127) date the Karoo lavas to 183 +/- 1 Ma and write that 'Seafloor spreading and dispersion of east and west Gondwana followed some 10-20 m.y. afterward.' Each piece broke off at a different time, tens of millions of years apart.

claim: The South Atlantic opened from south to north, like a zipper. Rifting began in the south in the Late Jurassic. Seafloor spreading started in the southern segment around 138-127 million years ago, and the last connection near the equator broke around 104-103 million years ago.
spoken_form: And the Atlantic between Africa and South America unzipped from the bottom up. The south tore open first. The last seam, near the equator, didn't let go for another twenty-five million years or so.
display: THE ATLANTIC UNZIPPED SOUTH TO NORTH
source_title: Torsvik, T. H. et al. (2009). A new scheme for the opening of the South Atlantic Ocean and the dissection of an Aptian salt basin. Geophys. J. Int. 177: 1315-1333; Heine, C., Zoethout, J. & Muller, R. D. (2013). Kinematics of the South Atlantic rift. Solid Earth 4: 215-253
quote: Rifting began in the south in the late Jurassic ... incorporating south-to-north opening of the ocean [Torsvik 2009] ... Final break-up between South America and Africa occurred in the conjugate Santos-Benguela margin segment at around 113 Ma and in the equatorial Atlantic domain between the Ghanaian Ridge and the Piaui-Ceara margin at 103 Ma. [Heine 2013]
caveat: 'Zipper' is our metaphor. In detail the opening was diachronous and happened in phases; within the central segment, Heine et al. find break-up began first in the Sergipe-Alagoas segment (in the north). Heine dates the start of normal seafloor spreading in the southern segment to around 127 Ma, with spreading beginning in isolated compartments in the far south around 138 Ma. The Torsvik quotes are extracted clauses because the full sentence is over 125 characters. Jokat 2003 dates the first South Atlantic oceanic crust to chron M9N (~130 Ma).

claim: When Gondwana broke up, Antarctica stayed almost still while the other pieces moved away. Africa and Australia moved at 2-4 cm (about 1-1.5 inches) a year. India raced at 18-20 cm (about 7-8 inches) a year in the Late Cretaceous, then slowed to about 5 cm a year after hitting Asia about 50 million years ago. One proposed reason: India's lithospheric root is only about 100 km deep, against 180-300 km for its siblings.
spoken_form: Antarctica barely moved. Everyone else left. And India sprinted, up to about eight inches a year, several times faster than Africa or Australia, until it slammed into Asia.
source_title: Kumar, P. et al. (2007). The rapid drift of the Indian tectonic plate. Nature 449: 894-897 (abstract via Europe PMC)
quote: Plate reconstructions based on palaeomagnetic data suggest that the Indian plate attained a very high speed (18-20 cm yr(-1) during the late Cretaceous period) subsequent to its breakup from Gondwanaland, and then slowed to approximately 5 cm yr(-1) after the continental collision with Asia approximately 50 Myr ago. The Australian and African plates moved comparatively less distance and at much lower speeds of 2-4 cm yr(-1) (refs 3-5). Antarctica remained almost stationary.
caveat: The speeds come from paleomagnetic reconstructions; later work (e.g. van Hinsbergen et al. 2011) finds similar peaks (~15-18 cm/yr). The thin-root explanation is the authors' hypothesis. India separated from Madagascar about 88 Ma (Storey et al. 1995, Science 267: 852).

claim: A 2022 paper argues the cause runs the opposite way to what you'd guess. South America was already wedge-shaped when Gondwana split, and that southward taper controlled how the South Atlantic opened, making the opening asymmetric and faster and wider in the south. The paper treats the taper as a starting condition and does not explain where it came from.
spoken_form: One recent study flips the question around. It argues South America's wedge shape didn't come from the Atlantic opening. The wedge was already there, and it steered how the ocean opened, wider and faster in the south.
source_title: Gao, D. (2022). Continental tapering of South America caused asymmetric non-uniform opening of the South Atlantic Ocean. Communications Earth & Environment 3: 278, doi:10.1038/s43247-022-00587-3
quote: Here I use geological and geophysical data to inform analytical modelling, revealing that westward drifting and southward tapering of the South American continent have controlled the asymmetry and the non-uniformity in South Atlantic opening. ... The splitting of the supercontinent to the tapering continent of South America set the initial boundary condition for South Atlantic opening.
caveat: The high confidence is about what the paper says, not that the question is settled. It is a single-author analytical model (West Virginia University), and it also claims its mechanism 'undermines the classical theory of thermal convection and upwelling as active drivers', which is a minority position. Cite it only in the direction taper -> opening. Owner override: no citation in the video; say 'one recent study'.

claim: The best expert answer we found: the southward points of Africa, South America and India are largely a legacy of Gondwana's breakup. The pieces drifted apart but kept their orientation, so their points still aim toward the South Pole, where they were once joined to Antarctica. Australia, from the same breakup, 'points' north, and smaller peninsulas have no single explanation. We found no peer-reviewed study that sets out to explain the taper itself.
spoken_form: So here's the honest answer most geologists would give. The big drips are scars. Africa, South America and India broke off a supercontinent built around Antarctica, and they still point back toward where they tore away. The small drips? No single answer.
source_title: Geological Society of London, 'Ask a Geologist: Why Do Most Peninsulas Point South?', answered by Ted Nield (editor, Geoscientist), c. 2009
quote: largely a legacy of the breakup of Gondwana ... drifted away from each other while preserving their general orientation, with the "point" directed to the South Pole ... to my eyes at least "points" north
caveat: The GSL page now redirects. The quote fragments come from the search engine's index of the page, not a live read (web.archive.org was unreachable). Nield also says peninsulas 'can have no single geological explanation', and gives Cape York, Arnhem Land and the Kola Peninsula as examples that point north. 'No peer-reviewed study explains the taper' comes from our own literature search: Gao 2022 takes the taper as given.

claim: Continents split along branching rifts that meet at triple junctions, and you can watch one happening now. In Afar, Ethiopia, a Y-shaped rift system is tearing Arabia away from Africa while Africa itself starts to split. Rifts that meet at angles cut continents into wedge-shaped pieces.
spoken_form: You can watch a continent being cut into wedges right now. In Ethiopia, three cracks meet in a giant Y. One arm made the Red Sea, one the Gulf of Aden, and the third is slowly unzipping East Africa.
display: AFAR: A CONTINENT CRACKING IN A 'Y'
source_title: Geological Society of London, Plate Tectonics: 'Triple Junction: The Red Sea/East Africa'
quote: The Afar region in Northern Ethiopia is the centre of a "Y" shaped rift system, where the continental lithosphere is being stretched and is splitting. ... The point in the Afar region where the boundaries of all three plates meet is called a Triple Junction.
caveat: The Afar facts are solid. 'Rifts meeting at angles make wedges' is a geometric inference, not a published explanation of the southern tapers. Burke & Dewey (1973, J. Geol. 81: 406-433) proposed that mantle plumes generate rift-rift-rift junctions, and the Benue Trough in Nigeria is often called the failed third arm of the South Atlantic junction, but that model is debated.

claim: Greenland's point has a different origin from the Gondwana tips. Greenland sits between two branches of North Atlantic rifting: the now-extinct Labrador Sea-Baffin Bay rift to the west (spreading from about 62 million years ago) and the North Atlantic to the east (breakup about 54-56 million years ago). Conventional models have Greenland drifting as its own plate in the Paleogene, which some geologists dispute.
spoken_form: Greenland's point is a different scar. About sixty million years ago, it was caught between two cracks: one opening the Labrador Sea toward Canada, the other the Atlantic toward Europe. Both were wider in the south. The result is a wedge pointing south.
source_title: Pulvertaft, T. C. R. & Dawes, P. R. (2011). North Atlantic spreading axes terminate in the continental cul-de-sacs of Baffin Bay and the Laptev Sea. Canadian Journal of Earth Sciences 48(3): 593-601 (GEUS abstract); see also Oakey & Chalmers (2012), JGR 117, doi:10.1029/2011JB008942
quote: In conventional plate-tectonic models, an independent Greenland plate is supposed to have drifted in the Paleogene along a transform fault through Nares Strait that links the two branches of the North Atlantic spreading system.
caveat: Pulvertaft & Dawes themselves argue against the independent plate. The ~62 Ma (chron 27) start of Labrador Sea spreading and the ~54-56 Ma NE Atlantic breakup come from search summaries of Oakey & Chalmers 2012 and NGU work, not from text I read verbatim. 'Both rifts widen south, making the wedge' is our interpretation (the geography does narrow northward at Davis/Nares Strait and Fram Strait). Labrador Sea spreading stopped in the Eocene-Oligocene (dates vary from 45 to 33 Ma).

claim: Baja California has a separate, young cause. About 6 million years ago the Pacific-North America plate boundary moved into the Gulf of California, and since then the Pacific Plate has carried Baja at least 276 km (about 170 miles) away from mainland Mexico.
spoken_form: Baja is a different story entirely. About six million years ago, the Pacific Plate grabbed it and started dragging it away from Mexico. It's moved at least a hundred and seventy miles so far, and it's still going.
display: BAJA: TORN AWAY ~6 MILLION YEARS AGO
source_title: Oskin, M. & Stock, J. (2003). Pacific-North America plate motion and opening of the Upper Delfin basin, northern Gulf of California, Mexico. GSA Bulletin 115(10): 1173-1190 (Caltech abstract)
quote: Addition of deformation from the continental margins of this basin indicates at least 276 +/- 13 km of Pacific-North America plate motion between coastal Sonora and the main gulf escarpment in Baja California since ca. 6 Ma ... but require that the Pacific-North America plate boundary became localized in the gulf at ca. 6 Ma.
caveat: Rifting in a proto-Gulf began earlier (~12 Ma), and true seafloor spreading in some gulf basins began only ~3.5 Ma. Say 'about six million years ago' for the main tear. Current motion is roughly 45-50 mm/yr (about 2 in/yr).

claim: Florida isn't a rift fragment at all. It is the exposed top of a huge carbonate platform: a tall underwater plateau of limestone and dolomite 2-6 km (about 1.25-3.75 miles) thick. Reef organisms built it in warm, shallow seas like today's Bahamas while its basement slowly sank, between about 180 and 60 million years ago.
spoken_form: And Florida? It's not a drip at all. It's the top of a gigantic reef. Up to nearly four miles of limestone, built by tiny sea creatures in warm shallow water, like the Bahamas today.
display: FLORIDA: UP TO ~4 MILES OF REEF ROCK
source_title: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Gulf of Mexico 2018 expedition log (1 May): the Florida Escarpment
quote: The Florida Escarpment is the western edge of a large carbonate platform that encompasses the Florida Peninsula. The platform is a tall underwater plateau (Figure 3) composed of carbonate rocks that were produced by biological organisms in warm, shallow, and tropical waters, very similar to the modern islands of the Bahamas. ... a platform of limestone and dolomite rock, with intermittent salt layers, that is between two and six kilometers (~1.25 and 3.75 miles) thick.
caveat: The dry-land outline of the peninsula is set mainly by sea level on top of the platform, and the platform is much wider than the peninsula. NOAA's Figure 3 is 'courtesy of A. Hine, 2009', so it is not public domain.

claim: Under Florida's limestone is basement rock that started out in Gondwana, next to West Africa (or South America). Its zircon ages match African and South American mountain-building events. That piece stayed attached to North America when Pangaea split.
spoken_form: But dig under the limestone and there's a twist. Florida's deepest bedrock started out on the other side of the Atlantic, next to West Africa, as a piece of Gondwana that got left behind.
source_title: Mueller, P. A. et al. (1994). Precambrian zircons from the Florida basement: A Gondwanan connection. Geology 22: 119-122 (USGS publication record)
quote: clearly places the basement of Florida in Gondwanaland proximal to the West African and/or Trans-Amazonian-San Luis cratons
caveat: Clause-level quote (the full sentence is over 125 characters). The Suwannee terrane joined North America while Pangaea was assembling (Paleozoic) and stayed when the Atlantic opened. Say 'next to West Africa', not 'a piece of Africa'.

claim: Is there a deep reason the land piled up in the north? One leading model says mantle convection alternates between two patterns. When continents are scattered it is lopsided ('degree-1': one hemisphere upwelling, the other sinking); when a supercontinent exists it is two-sided ('degree-2'). Today's mantle is largely the two-sided kind, with superplumes under Africa and the Pacific, so there is no evidence of a one-sided mantle forcing land north today. The current northern bias is best treated as a snapshot of drifting plates.
spoken_form: Is something deep inside Earth pushing the land north? Some models say the mantle can churn lopsided, up on one side and down on the other. But today's mantle isn't built that way. Most likely, this is just one frame of a very slow movie.
source_title: Zhong, S., Zhang, N., Li, Z.-X. & Roberts, J. H. (2007). Supercontinent cycles, true polar wander, and very long-wavelength mantle convection. Earth and Planetary Science Letters 261: 551-564
quote: mobile-lid mantle convection ... is characterized by either a spherical harmonic degree-1 planform with a major upwelling in one hemisphere and a major downwelling in the other hemisphere when continents are absent, or a degree-2 planform with two antipodal major upwellings when a supercontinent is present. ... Our model suggests that the largely degree-2 structure for the present-day mantle with the Africa and Pacific antipodal superplumes, is a natural consequence of this dynamic process
caveat: Abstract read from a repository mirror (geologyscience.ru) of the Elsevier abstract. 'No evidence that a one-sided mantle is forcing land north today' is our inference, not the paper's claim; there is no consensus deep cause. In the late Paleozoic, Gondwana sat over the South Pole (NASA). Kumar 2007 notes that Antarctica stayed put while Africa, India and Australia moved away. Geoscience Australia says Australia's plate 'travels around seven centimetres each year' (to the north-east).

claim: Real geology does have drips. Under California's southern Sierra Nevada, the dense root of the mountains has been peeling off and sinking into the mantle as a 'drip' beneath the Great Valley. This Rayleigh-Taylor instability began 10 to 3 million years ago.
spoken_form: Here's the strangest part. Continental drip started as a joke, but geologists have since found real drips. Under California's Sierra Nevada, the heavy root of the mountains is peeling off and sinking slowly into the Earth.
display: REAL DRIP: UNDER THE SIERRA NEVADA
source_title: Zandt, G. et al. (2004). Active foundering of a continental arc root beneath the southern Sierra Nevada in California. Nature 431: 41-46 (abstract via Europe PMC)
quote: The removal appears to have initiated between 10 and 3 Myr ago with a Rayleigh-Taylor-type instability, but with a pronounced asymmetric flow into a mantle downwelling (drip) beneath the adjacent Great Valley.
caveat: These drips sink downward into the mantle and have nothing to do with continents pointing south. Frame them as an ironic twist, not an explanation.

claim: In 2009, seismologists found a cold blob of lithosphere dripping into the mantle beneath central Nevada. It is about 100 km wide and at least 500 km tall (about 60 by 300 miles), and was described as 'honey dripping off a spoon'. The lead scientist admitted he had long been 'anti-drip'.
spoken_form: And under Nevada sits a drip about sixty miles wide and at least three hundred miles tall, like honey sliding off a spoon. The scientist who found it admitted he'd been anti-drip his whole career.
display: NEVADA DRIP: 60 MI WIDE, 300+ MI DEEP
source_title: ScienceDaily / NSF-ASU release (26 May 2009) on West, J. D., Fouch, M. J., Roth, J. B. & Elkins-Tanton, L. T. (2009). Vertical mantle flow associated with a lithospheric drip beneath the Great Basin. Nature Geoscience 2: 439-444
quote: A lithospheric drip can be envisioned as honey dripping off a spoon, where an initial lithospheric blob is followed by a long tail of material. ... a large cylindrical mass 100 km wide and at least 500 km tall (about 60 by 300 miles). "As a general rule, I have been anti-drip since my early days as a scientist," admits Fouch.
caveat: This is a press release about a peer-reviewed paper (Crossref: Nat. Geosci. 2: 439-444, doi:10.1038/ngeo526). The team thinks the drip started 15-20 million years ago and has little surface effect. The interpretation has been debated.

claim: In Turkey's Central Anatolia, a 2024 study links the rapidly sinking Konya Basin to a lithospheric drip inside a rising plateau. A 2022 study by the same group attributes basins on the Andes' Puna Plateau (e.g. the Arizaro Basin) to similar dripping.
spoken_form: Turkey has one too. A basin in the middle of a rising plateau is sinking, and lab models suggest a drip of rock is pulling it down from below.
display: TURKEY: A BASIN PULLED DOWN FROM BELOW
source_title: Andersen, A. J., Gogus, O. H., Pysklywec, R. N., Sengul Uluocak, E. & Santimano, T. (2024). Multistage lithospheric drips control active basin formation within an uplifting orogenic plateau. Nature Communications 15 (abstract via Europe PMC); Andersen et al. (2022), Communications Earth & Environment 3: 150
quote: Using scaled laboratory (analogue) experiments we show that the active formation of the Konya Basin may be accounted for by the descent of a mantle lithospheric drip causing local circular-shaped surface subsidence. We interpret that the Konya Basin is developing through a secondary drip pulse that is contemporaneous with broad plateau uplift caused by a larger-scale lithospheric drip since the Miocene.
caveat: The subsidence is measured (GNSS/InSAR); the drip is an interpretation based on models ('may be accounted for'). The 2022 Andes abstract says 'the formation of the Arizaro Basin and nearby Central Andean basins are caused by symptomatic lithospheric dripping events' (from analogue models).

claim: Pangaea Proxima, first named 'Pangaea Ultima', is Christopher Scotese's future-supercontinent model. In it the Atlantic stops widening and closes, and the Americas rejoin Europe and Africa in about 250 million years. It is a model scenario, not a prediction.
spoken_form: One model, from geologist Christopher Scotese, has the Atlantic slamming shut and America crashing back into Africa in about two hundred fifty million years.
source_title: Pangaea Proxima (Wikipedia, citing Scotese 2003/2021, Williams & Nield, New Scientist 2007). Cross-check: NASA APOD 2 Oct 2000, 'Pangea Ultima: Earth in 250 Million Years?' (Credit & Copyright: C. R. Scotese, PALEOMAP)
quote: This potential configuration, hypothesized by Christopher Scotese in November 1982, earned its name from its similarity to the ancient Pangaea supercontinent.
caveat: The 1982 date comes only from Wikipedia; the primary Paleomap page (scotese.com) was unreachable. The 250-Myr timescale and the Atlantic closing are confirmed by APOD 2000 and Scotese's own Paleomap material. Scotese's maps are copyrighted, so redraw the configuration with the engine and label it 'MODEL'.

claim: Scotese first called the future supercontinent 'Pangaea Ultima' ('Last Pangaea'). He later renamed it 'Pangaea Proxima' ('Next Pangaea') because 'Ultima' suggested it would be the last supercontinent ever.
spoken_form: He first called it Pangaea Ultima, the last Pangaea. Then he renamed it, because the planet clearly isn't done.
source_title: Pangaea Proxima (Wikipedia, lead section, citing Williams & Nield 2007)
quote: could imply that it would be the last-ever supercontinent
caveat: No date for the rename is known. The 2023 Farnsworth study still uses the name 'Pangea Ultima' for this configuration, so both names are in use and the narration should pick one.

claim: Novopangaea was proposed by Roy Livermore in the late 1990s. Today's motions continue: the Atlantic keeps opening and the Pacific closes. The Americas hit Antarctica, which is drifting north, and then hit Africa-Eurasia. Davies, Green & Duarte (2018) rate it the most likely of the four scenarios.
spoken_form: In the model most of these geologists bet on, nothing changes direction. The Pacific closes, and the Americas crash into Antarctica.
source_title: Davies, Green & Duarte, 'What planet Earth might look like when the next supercontinent forms – four scenarios' (Bangor University / The Conversation, 27 Nov 2018), summarizing Global and Planetary Change 169:133–144 (2018). Proposer: Novopangaea (Wikipedia).
quote: Of these four scenarios we believe that Novopangea is the most likely.
caveat: 'Most likely' is the opinion of three authors, not a consensus. The Livermore/late-1990s attribution comes from Wikipedia, so treat it as medium. Spellings vary: Novopangaea and Novopangea.

claim: Amasia: Yale researchers (Mitchell, Kilian & Evans, Nature, 9 Feb 2012) model the Arctic Ocean and Caribbean closing first, with the Americas meeting Eurasia near the North Pole in 50–200 million years. A different Amasia model from Curtin University (Huang et al., National Science Review, 2022) forms it by closing the Pacific in 200–300 million years.
spoken_form: Another model sends everything north. The Arctic Ocean vanishes, and America meets Asia practically at the North Pole.
source_title: Yale News, 'Next supercontinent forms: Arctic Ocean, Caribbean will vanish first' (8 Feb 2012); Phys.org/Curtin University (30 Sep 2022)
quote: You'd have the Americas meeting Eurasia practically at the North Pole.
caveat: The 50–200 Myr figure was Mitchell speaking to Yale News; the paper itself gives no date. The name 'Amasia' was coined earlier by Paul F. Hoffman (Wikipedia). The 2012 and 2022 Amasias are different models with the same name. Yale: Antarctica may stay separate.

claim: Aurica (Duarte, Schellart & Rosas, Geological Magazine, 2016): both the Atlantic and the Pacific close, a new ocean opens across Asia, and Australia ends up at the centre. The name joins Australia and America.
spoken_form: A third model closes both oceans at once and puts Australia in the middle of everything. Its name is Australia plus America: Aurica.
source_title: Bangor University / The Conversation (27 Nov 2018); Duarte, Schellart & Rosas, Geological Magazine 155:45–58, doi:10.1017/S0016756816000716; Aurica (Wikipedia) for the name
quote: it would be at the centre of the new continent as East Asia and the Americas close the Pacific from either side
caveat: It requires new subduction zones in the Atlantic, which the authors say may already be starting off SW Iberia, but this is speculative. The name's derivation is from Wikipedia and Portuguese press, so medium.

claim: The next supercontinent has been suggested to form in about 200–250 million years. All four named supercontinents are competing computer and geological model scenarios, and the authors call them speculative.
spoken_form: Geologists think the next supercontinent arrives in about two hundred to two hundred fifty million years. They just can't agree on what it looks like.
source_title: Davies, Green & Duarte, Bangor University news (27 Nov 2018)
quote: It has been suggested that the next supercontinent will form in 200-250 million years.
caveat: The time range depends on the model; Amasia's estimates run from 50 to 300 million years. Ronald Blakey (quoted in The Atlantic, 2013) calls projections beyond about 100 million years 'very, very speculative'. Present all four maps as labelled models.

claim: Farnsworth et al. 2023 (Nature Geoscience) simulated the 'Pangea Ultima' supercontinent about 250 million years from now. Only 8–16% of land stayed habitable for mammals, with widespread temperatures of 40–50 °C (104–122 °F). The model assumes humans stop burning fossil fuels.
spoken_form: One study ran the climate on that future supercontinent. Only about one-tenth of the land stayed livable for mammals, with heat over a hundred and twenty degrees.
source_title: University of Bristol press release, 'New research reveals extreme heat likely to wipe out humans and mammals in the distant future' (25 Sep 2023), on Farnsworth et al., Nature Geoscience 16:901–908, doi:10.1038/s41561-023-01259-3
quote: only somewhere between 8% and 16% of land would be habitable for mammals
caveat: This is one study using one geography, Scotese's Ultima/Proxima. Brief rule: say 'one study'. Other quotes: 'Widespread temperatures of between 40 to 50 degrees Celsius', and Mills: 'this assumes that humans will stop burning fossil fuels'. It projects heat stress, not proven extinction.

claim: Where the US ends up depends on the model. Proxima/Ultima: back against Europe and Africa. Amasia: up against Asia over the Arctic. Novopangaea: the Americas hit Antarctica, then Africa-Eurasia. Aurica: the Americas and East Asia close around Australia.
spoken_form: So which continent does America crash into? Depending on the model: Africa, Asia, Antarctica, or Australia. Pick your neighbor.
display: US crashes into: Africa? Asia? Antarctica? Australia?
source_title: Davies, Green & Duarte, Bangor University news (27 Nov 2018); Yale News (2012)
quote: leading to a reforming of Pangea as the Americas, Europe and Africa are brought back together
caveat: This is a synthesis of four model descriptions; each map must be labelled 'MODEL'. The 'pick your neighbor' joke is fine as long as the four-way uncertainty is clear.

claim: USGS: tectonic plates move at roughly the rate your fingernails grow, and GPS can track that motion to within a fraction of a millimetre per year.
spoken_form: Continents move about as fast as your fingernails grow.
source_title: USGS FAQ, 'How fast do tectonic plates move?'
quote: Tectonic plates move roughly at the same rate that your fingernails grow.
caveat: This is an approximation; plate speeds range from under 1 inch to about 6 inches a year. A 1988 NASA JPL release made the same fingernail comparison.

claim: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads about 2.5 cm (about 1 inch) per year. The fastest ridge, the East Pacific Rise near Easter Island, spreads more than 15 cm (about 6 inches) per year. The slowest, the Arctic Ridge, spreads less than 2.5 cm per year.
spoken_form: The Atlantic widens by about an inch a year. Parts of the Pacific floor race along at six.
source_title: USGS, This Dynamic Earth, 'Understanding plate motions'
quote: The rate of spreading along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge averages about 2.5 centimeters per year (cm/yr), or 25 km in a million years.
caveat: These are full spreading rates (both sides combined). The figures are long-term averages from magnetic stripes. Same page: 'The Arctic Ridge has the slowest rate (less than 2.5 cm/yr), and the East Pacific Rise... has the fastest rate (more than 15 cm/yr).'

claim: Fingernails grow about 3.47 mm a month (about 1.6 inches a year) and toenails about 1.62 mm a month (about 0.8 inches a year). This is a small study of 22 healthy American young adults.
spoken_form: Your fingernails grow about an inch and a half a year. Your toenails, less than half that.
source_title: Yaemsiri et al., 'Growth rate of human fingernails and toenails in healthy American young adults', J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 24(4):420–423 (2010)
quote: average fingernail growth rate was faster than that of toenails (3.47 vs. 1.62 mm/month, P < 0.01)
caveat: Conversions are computed (3.47 mm × 12 = 4.16 cm/yr = 1.64 in; 1.62 mm × 12 = 1.94 cm/yr = 0.77 in). The sample of n=22 is small, and growth varies with the person and the finger.

claim: The two US science agencies pick different nails. NOAA says land masses move about 1.5 cm (0.6 inches) a year on average, 'about the rate that human toenails grow'. USGS says fingernails.
spoken_form: Even the government can't agree. One agency says continents move at fingernail speed. Another says toenails.
source_title: NOAA National Ocean Service, 'What is plate tectonics?' (oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/tectonics.html); USGS FAQ
quote: Earth's land masses move toward and away from each other at an average rate of about 1.5 centimeters (0.6 inches) a year. That's about the rate that human toenails grow!
caveat: Both are fair, since they describe different averages. It is a joke beat, not a contradiction to fact-check. Do not name agencies on screen (owner override); 'one agency... another' works.

claim: The Americas and Africa/Europe separate at about 4 cm (about 1.5 inches) a year, which is fingernail speed. A South Atlantic drilling site off South America and Africa (IODP U1558, about 31°S) records a half-spreading rate of about 19.5 mm/yr, a full rate of about 39 mm/yr.
spoken_form: Africa and South America are still drifting apart, about an inch and a half every year. That's exactly fingernail speed.
source_title: University of Southampton press release via EurekAlert (27 Jan 2021) on Wang et al., Nature, doi:10.1038/s41586-020-03139-x; IODP Expedition 390/393 Proceedings, Site U1558 (2024)
quote: The plates attached to the Americas are moving apart from those attached to Europe and Africa by four centimetres per year.
caveat: Rates vary along the ridge, from about 3 to 4 cm/yr in the South Atlantic and lower in the North Atlantic (about 2.4 cm/yr North America–Africa per UCSD Earthguide). Say 'about an inch or so, up to an inch and a half'. IODP quote: 'a slow half spreading rate of ~19.5 mm/y'.

claim: COMPUTED: since Bacon noticed the fit in 1620 (406 years), the Atlantic has widened about 33–53 ft (10–16 m), roughly a school bus or more. And 250 million years at about 1.5 in/yr is about 6,200 miles (10,000 km), a quarter of the way around Earth.
spoken_form: Since Bacon noticed the fit, the Atlantic has grown about a school bus wider. Give it two hundred fifty million years at fingernail speed, and that adds up to a quarter of the way around the planet.
source_title: Computed from USGS This Dynamic Earth (2.5 cm/yr) and the Southampton/EurekAlert 2021 release (4 cm/yr)
quote: This rate may seem slow by human standards, but because this process has been going on for millions of years, it has resulted in plate movement of thousands of kilometers.
caveat: Pure arithmetic: 406 yr × 2.5–4 cm = 10.2–16.2 m (33–53 ft); 250e6 yr × 4 cm = 10,000 km = 6,214 mi = 25% of Earth's circumference. Real motion is not constant or straight-line, so use 'about'. A school bus is about 35–45 ft.

claim: North-up is only a convention. Medieval European world maps put east at the top: the Hereford Mappa Mundi (c. 1300) shows Eden at the top, in the east, with Jerusalem at the centre. 'Orient(ation)' comes from the east-up habit.
spoken_form: For centuries, European maps didn't even put north on top. They put east up, with the Garden of Eden at the top of the world.
source_title: Hereford Cathedral, The Mappa Mundi (themappamundi.co.uk)
quote: The earthly paradise, Eden, is represented by a circular island at the eastern extreme of the world (the top).
caveat: The 'orient' etymology (Latin oriens, 'rising', meaning east) was not verified against a dictionary because etymonline returned 403. Avoid the etymology line or soften it. Dating is c.1300; Commons metadata says c.1250.

claim: Al-Idrisi's world maps, made for King Roger II of Sicily and completed in 1154, put south at the top, following the Balkhi school.
spoken_form: And one of the greatest maps of the Middle Ages, drawn for a king of Sicily, put south at the top.
source_title: Library of Congress, Worlds Revealed blog, Carissa Pastuch, 'Al-Idrisi's Masterpiece of Medieval Geography' (Jan 2022)
quote: Following the Balkhi School of Geography, the maps are oriented with the South at the top and Mecca at the center.
caveat: The oldest surviving copy is c.1325 (BnF MS Arabe 2221); the 1154 original is lost. The Commons image (TabulaRogeriana.jpg) is Konrad Miller's 1929 composite, and the page asks users not to rotate it north-up.

claim: In 1979, 21-year-old Australian Stuart McArthur published the south-up 'McArthur's Universal Corrective Map of the World', to answer 'the perpetual onslaught of Down Under jokes'.
spoken_form: In nineteen seventy-nine, a twenty-one-year-old Australian got so sick of 'Down Under' jokes that he published a world map with Australia on top.
source_title: South-up map orientation (Wikipedia, citing Wood, Kaiser & Abramms, Seeing Through Maps, 2006, pp. 50–51, and the ICA Commission on Map Design 2014); ABC News Australia (8 Aug 2020)
quote: In 1979, twenty-one year old Australian Stuart McArthur published
caveat: Sources differ on his age and status (college or high-school student). The 26 Jan 1979 (Australia Day) launch appears only in secondary sources. The map is still in copyright, so do NOT show it; rotate our own globe south-up instead. The 'Down Under jokes' wording is also in ABC 2020.

claim: The most famous photo of Earth, Apollo 17's 'Blue Marble' (7 Dec 1972), was taken with the South Pole at the top. The version everyone knows was flipped north-up.
spoken_form: Even the most famous photo of Earth was taken with Antarctica on top. It got flipped, because that's how we're used to seeing it.
source_title: The Blue Marble (Wikipedia); Wikimedia Commons file 'Apollo 17 Blue Marble original orientation (AS17-148-22727).jpg' (NASA, public domain)
quote: The original photograph was taken with the South Pole facing the top.
caveat: Wikipedia's wording is somewhat inconsistent ('rotated with south pointing up relative to the capsule'). In zero-g the 'original orientation' is just how the camera was held, so say 'taken with Antarctica on top' and 'published flipped'. Strong visual: show both PD versions side by side.

claim: Myth-bust: the Cape of Good Hope is NOT Africa's southern tip. That is Cape Agulhas, about 90 miles (150 km) east-southeast, which is also the official IHO boundary between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
spoken_form: Ask anyone where Africa ends and they'll say the Cape of Good Hope. Wrong. The real tip is a quiet spot about ninety miles away called Cape Agulhas.
display: Real tip of Africa: Cape Agulhas
source_title: Cape of Good Hope (Wikipedia); Cape Agulhas (Wikipedia, citing IHO Special Publication 23, Limits of Oceans and Seas, 1953)
quote: A common misconception is that the Cape of Good Hope is the southern tip of Africa.
caveat: Same page: 'the southernmost point of Africa is Cape Agulhas about 150 kilometres (90 mi) to the east-southeast.' Agulhas is about 34 mi (55 km) farther south in latitude. Britannica was 403 and could not be checked directly; the facts are uncontroversial.

claim: The Cape of Good Hope's marker makes a carefully worded claim: 'the most south-western point of the African continent', not the southernmost point.
spoken_form: The sign at the Cape of Good Hope is very carefully worded. It doesn't say southernmost. It says most south-western.
source_title: Atlas Obscura, 'Cape of Good Hope' (search excerpt); 22places.com; German Wikivoyage ('südwestlichste Punkt Afrikas')
quote: The marker found at the Cape of Good Hope is slightly more contrived: the most southwestern point of the African continent.
caveat: Atlas Obscura returned 403 to the fetcher; the quote is from the search-engine excerpt, so the exact engraved text was not seen. Commons has photos of the sign (CC BY-SA). Check the sign text in the photo before quoting it on screen.

claim: Bartolomeu Dias, the first European to round it (1488), named it the 'Cape of Storms'. King John II of Portugal renamed it the 'Cape of Good Hope', an early rebrand driven by hope of a sea route to India.
spoken_form: And its original name? The Cape of Storms. A king renamed it the Cape of Good Hope. History's first rebrand.
display: Cape of Storms → Cape of Good Hope
source_title: Cape of Good Hope (Wikipedia, citing Britannica's Bartolomeu Dias entry)
quote: Bartolomeu Dias on 12 March 1488, who named it the "Cape of Storms"
caveat: Who renamed it is not fully settled: most sources say John II, and some say Dias himself. Say 'Portugal renamed it' to be safe. Dates differ slightly (late 1487 / early 1488). Calling it 'history's first rebrand' is a joke, not a factual claim.

claim: 'Agulhas' means 'needles'. The Portuguese named it the Cape of Needles because around 1500 the compass needle there pointed exactly at true north. So the southern tip of Africa is named after a needle pointing north.
spoken_form: Its name means Cape of Needles, because sailors' compass needles there pointed perfectly north. Africa's southern tip is named after pointing north.
source_title: Cape Agulhas (Wikipedia, citing Patricia Seed on the coincidence of magnetic and true north)
quote: the direction of magnetic north (and therefore the compass needle) coincided with true north in the region
caveat: Some sources (Britannica, as cited in search results) give a second explanation: needle-like reefs and rocks. Hedge it: 'the best-known story is…'. Magnetic declination there is very different today.

claim: Cape Horn is not named for a horn shape. It is named after the Dutch town of Hoorn, home and sponsor of the expedition that first rounded it on 29 January 1616. The expedition's second ship, also called Hoorn, had burned down while its hull was being scorched clean.
spoken_form: Cape Horn isn't shaped like a horn. It's named after a Dutch town called Hoorn. The explorers' other ship, also called the Hoorn, had accidentally burned down while they were cleaning it.
source_title: New Netherland Institute, 'Cape Horn: How a Trading Monopoly, a Disenchanted Wealthy Merchant, and Two Dutch Explorers Put it on the Map'
quote: During a refit, the Hoorn was lost, having caught fire while her weed-fouled hull was being scorched clean.
caveat: Same page: 'On January 29, 1616, the Eendracht rounded "Kaap Hoorn."' Some sources say the name honours both the town and the ship; the town is the primary namesake. Explorers: Willem Schouten and Jacob Le Maire.

claim: Cape Horn sailor tradition: a sailor who had rounded the Horn could wear a gold loop earring and eat with one leg on the table. National Geographic also lists the nickname 'tailbone of the Americas'.
spoken_form: Sailors who survived rounding Cape Horn earned the right to wear a gold earring and eat with one foot on the table. Some call it the tailbone of the Americas.
source_title: National Geographic Travel, 'Bottoms Up on Cape Horn, Chile'; Cape Horn (Wikipedia)
quote: wear a gold loop earring and to dine with one leg on the table
caveat: This is sea lore and tradition, not a documented rule; sources disagree on which ear. Wikipedia: 'Traditionally, a sailor who had rounded the Horn was entitled to wear a gold loop earring'. Frame it as 'tradition says'. No reliable source was found for 'record winds at Cape Horn', so that line was dropped; NatGeo says only that the latitude's winds are the 'furious fifties'.

claim: Cape Horn is not on the South American mainland. It sits on Hornos Island, which was only found to be an island in 1624, and it is not even South America's southernmost point; Águila Islet is farther south.
spoken_form: And the famous tip of South America? It's on an island. And it's not even the southernmost point.
display: Cape Horn: an island, not the tip
source_title: Cape Horn (Wikipedia)
quote: Although not the most southerly point of South America (which is Águila Islet) ... it was only in 1624 that the Horn was discovered to be an island
caveat: Águila Islet is in the Diego Ramírez Islands, far offshore; the mainland's southern tip is Cape Froward (not verified here). The Commons photo '00 4479 Cape Horn.jpg' wrongly describes Cape Horn as the mainland tip, so ignore that caption.

claim: Kanyakumari (Cape Comorin) is the southern tip of mainland India, but India's southernmost point is Indira Point on Great Nicobar Island. In the 2004 earthquake and tsunami, that tip sank about 4.25 m (14 ft).
spoken_form: India's southern tip on the mainland is Kanyakumari. But the country's true southernmost point is on an island, and in two thousand four, it sank about fourteen feet.
source_title: Indira Point (Wikipedia); Kanyakumari (Wikipedia)
quote: the southernmost tip subsided 4.25 metres (13.9 ft) after the earthquake
caveat: This is a Wikipedia-level source. The 'lighthouse now underwater' claims are from aggregator sites and could not be confirmed. Since the drip's India tip is Kanyakumari, use this only as a side gag, or skip it.

claim: Greenland, one of the drip's tips and where Wegener died, was named as a marketing move. Erik the Red said people would be keener to settle there if the land had an attractive name.
spoken_form: Greenland got its name from a Viking marketing campaign. Erik the Red said people would want to move there if it had a nice name.
source_title: Eirik the Red's Saga, tr. J. Sephton (1880), Project Gutenberg #17946
quote: men will desire much the more to go there if the land has a good name.
caveat: The quote is verbatim from the saga translation; the saga is literature written about 200 years later, so say 'according to the saga'. Some argue southern Greenland's coast is genuinely green in summer; Snopes covers this.

claim: Florida's famous 'Southernmost Point' buoy in Key West is not the continental US's southernmost point, and not even Key West's. The real one is Ballast Key, a private island about 10 miles (16 km) away.
spoken_form: Florida's famous Southernmost Point marker? Not the southernmost point. The real one is a private island ten miles away.
source_title: Southernmost Point Buoy (Wikipedia, citing the City of Key West buoy history and others)
quote: neither the true southernmost point of the continental US nor of Key West
caveat: Key West's own true southern tip is on US Navy (Truman Annex) land, about 900 ft farther south. The buoy was installed 10 Sep 1983. 'Continental US' here means the contiguous 48 states.

claim: Green's 1875 book draws the 'normal form of a continent' as a three-lobed triangle (Figure 1) and labels a figure 'Tetrahedral collapse of Earth's crust in the southern hemisphere' (Figure 5), with S. America, Africa and Australia at the corners of a six-faced tetrahedron.
spoken_form: In his eighteen seventy-five book, Green drew what he called the normal shape of a continent: a triangle pointing south.
display: Green, 1875: 'the normal form of a continent'
source_title: W. Lowthian Green, Vestiges of the Molten Globe (London: E. Stanford, 1875), archive.org scan (Oxford copy, Google-digitized), p. 5–6 and Figures 1, 4, 5
quote: This figure represents the normal form of a continent in its simplest development, namely, as a regular trilobed mass.
caveat: Figure pages: Figure 1 = scan leaf n17; Figures 4–5 = n39; Figures 7–10 (globes) = n56–n57. archive.org marks the scan 'NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT'. The folded Plates I–II are cut off in this scan. 300-dpi renders are saved in .../research-future-visuals/assets/.

claim: In 1858 Antonio Snider-Pellegrini published a two-panel map showing the Americas and Africa fitted together and then pulled apart: the first known illustration of the Atlantic opening.
spoken_form: In eighteen fifty-eight, a Frenchman drew the Americas and Africa snapped together like puzzle pieces. Then he pulled them apart.
source_title: Wikimedia Commons, File:Antonio Snider-Pellegrini Opening of the Atlantic.jpg (from La Création et ses mystères dévoilés, Paris, 1858)
quote: First known illustration of the Opening of the Atlantic Ocean, by Antonio Snider-Pellegrini, 1858.
caveat: He tied the split to the Biblical Flood, so do not present him as a proto-plate-tectonics scientist. He was an American-born geographer working in Paris; 'a Frenchman' is loose, so prefer 'a geographer in Paris'.
